frictionVectors.title: EU gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing for market reforms and greater supply flexibility. Algiers is using energy ties to preserve strategic autonomy and diplomatic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara tensions
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for the Polisario Front keeps relations with Morocco deeply adversarial. The rivalry complicates Maghreb trade, energy coordination, and regional security.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Repayment obligations and infrastructure ties with Chinese lenders continue to constrain fiscal room and policy flexibility. Luanda is seeking broader financing partnerships while protecting control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore production pressure
frictionVectors.details: Mature oil fields, declining output risks, and the energy transition threaten the revenue base. Foreign operators remain essential for capital and technical capacity, limiting near-term resource autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Northern jihadist spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity moving south from the Sahel is placing pressure on Benin's northern border and transport corridors. Security dependence on external partners is increasing as the government seeks to protect trade and extractive zones.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's role as a regional gateway is exposed to political and commercial competition from neighboring ports. Foreign logistics, financing, and customs interests remain influential in the corridor's development.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains significant negotiating leverage with major diamond firms, but its fiscal model remains vulnerable to global demand shifts and synthetic stones. The government is pressing for greater local cutting, processing, and downstream value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals could bring capital and technology but also intensify competition among Western, Chinese, and regional investors. Gaborone is seeking investment without surrendering regulatory control.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities are deepening ties with Russia while reducing reliance on France and other Western partners. This increases political room for maneuver but creates new risks around opaque security arrangements and external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal gold governance
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to formalize and nationalize gold purchasing aim to capture more value for the state, but insecurity and informal networks limit enforcement. Foreign and regional buyers remain active across a difficult-to-monitor supply chain.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and coltan leakage
frictionVectors.details: Weak oversight and informal cross-border networks allow gold and tantalum exports to bypass state controls. External traders and regional intermediaries capture much of the value.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-border economic friction
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Rwanda disrupt border commerce and complicate access to regional transport corridors. Burundi remains dependent on external routes and donor-backed infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is seeking to convert its Atlantic position into logistics and maritime-security leverage while balancing European, Chinese, and wider commercial interests. Its small market limits bargaining power over major infrastructure investors.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and water dependence
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains exposed to imported fuel, desalination costs, and climate stress. External finance is central to expanding renewable energy and resilient infrastructure.

highlights: Conflict and foreign capital erode control

frictionVectors.title: Oil, gas, and pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues and major projects remain vulnerable to foreign operators, opaque contracting, and infrastructure bottlenecks. The state retains formal ownership but has limited leverage over financing, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Separatist-zone infrastructure insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, agricultural supply chains, and investment. Instability increases reliance on security assistance and weakens national control over local economic networks.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond capture
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal mining and armed-group influence keep major mineral flows outside effective state regulation. Russian-linked security and commercial actors have expanded their influence around strategic sites and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and border vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on fragile routes through Cameroon and neighboring states for fuel, food, and exports. Armed groups and foreign security interests compete to shape access to these corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: State revenues remain heavily dependent on oil production and export infrastructure controlled through foreign technical and financial partnerships. Price volatility and opaque revenue management constrain sovereign development capacity.

frictionVectors.title: External security realignment
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown of French military involvement is reshaping Chad's external partnerships while instability in Sudan increases border pressure. Gulf, Russian, and regional actors may gain influence over security and logistics decisions.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: France’s control of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty grievance and limits Comoros’ influence over surrounding maritime resources and migration policy.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, and telecommunications development rely heavily on foreign financing, leaving the archipelago exposed to shifting Gulf, French, and other external priorities.

highlights: Critical minerals draw intense foreign competition
State authority remains fragmented in the east

frictionVectors.title: MINING SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and coltan supply chains remain vulnerable to opaque contracts, informal production, and foreign commercial leverage, limiting the state’s capture of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving armed groups and regional actors continues to threaten mining zones, transport routes, and Kinshasa’s ability to enforce national resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil operators and volatile production revenues constrain fiscal autonomy, while opaque contracting and debt-service obligations reduce domestic control over petroleum gains.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE–DEBT LINKAGES
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads and public works provide strategic connectivity but can tie future resource revenues and policy space to external creditors and contractors.

highlights: Commodity upgrading is improving bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Côte d’Ivoire has strengthened domestic regulation and processing ambitions, but multinational traders and overseas processors still capture substantial value from its cocoa sector.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan’s expanding logistics role and continued Western security ties increase resilience, while also creating exposure to external influence over critical transport and defense infrastructure.

highlights: Base diplomacy remains the core economic asset
Debt and logistics exposure constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and leverage but make Djibouti’s sovereignty highly dependent on rival external powers.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled port infrastructure and heavy debt exposure, particularly to Chinese-linked projects, limit the state’s room to manage strategic assets independently.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms, Gulf investment, and foreign currency needs increase outside leverage over major assets and economic policy. Egypt retains formal control but faces constrained bargaining space.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to upstream operating decisions and regional diplomatic competition over Nile governance.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Declining production increases dependence on foreign operators, technical partners, and external capital to sustain offshore output and LNG infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Regional gas competition
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea must compete with larger West African producers for LNG markets, investment, and shipping access while trying to preserve national control over declining resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production depends heavily on foreign firms, financing, and technical capacity, limiting Eritrea's ability to fully capture resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: External naval deployments and competition around the Red Sea increase the strategic value of Eritrean ports while exposing the country to pressure from Gulf and wider international actors.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, customs revenue, energy links, and transport access remain closely tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's autonomy over supply chains and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and timber exposure
frictionVectors.details: Agricultural exports remain vulnerable to external market rules, water constraints, and concentrated corporate ownership, restricting domestic control over land-based resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD gives Ethiopia greater strategic leverage over regional water and electricity systems, but unresolved tensions with Egypt and Sudan create persistent diplomatic and security risk.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on international lenders constrain Addis Ababa's policy autonomy, while foreign participation remains important for energy, telecoms, logistics, and industrial projects.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain fiscal anchors

frictionVectors.title: Mining and rail control
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities are pressing for greater Gabonese participation in manganese and infrastructure assets, while foreign operators remain central to production, rail logistics, and export capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector fiscal dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon retains leverage through hydrocarbons but remains vulnerable to declining mature fields, financing constraints, and dependence on external capital and technical expertise.

highlights: Senegal remains the strategic economic partner
Tourism and fisheries drive external exposure

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia transport dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal-linked corridors, border trade, and regional security cooperation, limiting its autonomy over transport and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak monitoring pressure marine resources, while port, energy, and tourism infrastructure remain dependent on outside finance and investment.

highlights: Gold and lithium policy turning more interventionist

frictionVectors.title: Galamsey and gold-chain leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining is degrading water and farmland while linking local networks to foreign buyers and equipment suppliers, undermining state control of the gold economy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is seeking greater local processing and value capture in lithium and other minerals, but financing needs and established multinational interests constrain negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou rail and port corridor
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project gives Guinea major strategic leverage but ties export capacity to large Chinese-linked and multinational infrastructure commitments, creating long-term sovereignty and revenue risks.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite concentration and contract opacity
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains dependent on foreign operators and external logistics for bauxite exports, while the transitional government’s contract reviews heighten tensions with investors and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau’s dominant export, while limited domestic infrastructure leaves farmers vulnerable to price and credit pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security and illicit flows
frictionVectors.details: Weak coastal enforcement increases exposure to illegal fishing and narcotics trafficking, with external networks exploiting limited state capacity and underdeveloped port infrastructure.

highlights: Mombasa corridor remains a contested gateway

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial Chinese infrastructure exposure limit Nairobi's room to redirect capital toward nationally controlled projects. Debt-service pressures continue to shape decisions on ports, rail, energy, and taxation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa faces competition from regional corridors and foreign-backed logistics networks. Control over transport infrastructure remains central to Kenya's bargaining power with neighboring states and external investors.

highlights: South African economic gravity remains dominant

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water revenues and infrastructure are strategically important but bind Lesotho tightly to South Africa through financing, contracts, and electricity interdependence. Delays and cost overruns can weaken sovereign control over the country's most valuable export.

frictionVectors.title: Textile-sector vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The export garment industry depends heavily on foreign firms and preferential market access. Changes in United States trade policy or investor decisions can rapidly affect employment and fiscal stability.

highlights: Port and shipping assets attract outside capital

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations, especially around Nimba and Bong-linked corridors, give foreign investors substantial influence over transport, employment, and export earnings. Weak domestic processing capacity limits Liberia's value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime governance
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port modernization and Liberia's major maritime registry connect national revenues to foreign operators, regulators, and shipping interests. Concession transparency and revenue retention remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

highlights: Oil wealth remains fragmented by rival authorities
Foreign military and commercial actors deepen competition

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon control and blockade risk
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security networks contest control over oil fields, export terminals, and the National Oil Corporation. Production interruptions remain a direct instrument of political bargaining and a threat to national revenue sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf states, Egypt, and European actors retain overlapping security and energy interests. Foreign-backed military positions and opaque commercial arrangements constrain unified Libyan control of infrastructure and borders.

highlights: Critical minerals draw intensified foreign interest

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral-project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects rely on foreign capital, technology, and export markets, particularly for nickel and cobalt. Energy costs, environmental pressures, and limited domestic processing reduce Madagascar's share of downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and local consent
frictionVectors.details: Port, road, and power infrastructure built around mining enclaves can bypass broader national development. Land disputes and community opposition create recurring friction over who controls resource-bearing areas and receives compensation.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed projects in uranium, graphite and rare earths offer export potential but raise concerns over fiscal terms, local processing and environmental oversight.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND IMPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, foreign-exchange constraints and reliance on external lenders limit Malawi's ability to secure power and manage strategic infrastructure independently.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SOVEREIGNTY DRIVE
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and revised terms in gold mining, creating friction with foreign operators while artisanal production remains difficult to regulate.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support expands Moscow's influence over political and security decisions as relations with France and Western institutions deteriorate.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS PARTNERSHIP
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international operators could strengthen state revenues, but requires careful management of cross-border governance and revenue expectations.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Rail and port capacity remain central to Mauritania's resource strategy, leaving the country exposed to foreign financiers, operators and commodity-price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS SOVEREIGNTY SETTLEMENT
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claims and negotiations over the Chagos Archipelago remain intertwined with the future of the Diego Garcia military facility and wider UK-US strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Investment and security partnerships involving India, China and Western states create opportunities but require careful balancing around port access, surveillance and undersea infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE POLITICS
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy projects in Western Sahara generate diplomatic and legal friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front and critics of Moroccan sovereignty claims.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND ENERGY SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding renewables, desalination and green-hydrogen capacity, but remains exposed to imported energy, water scarcity and foreign technology and capital.

highlights: LNG restart remains central to fiscal recovery
Cabo Delgado security still limits state control

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks and dependence on foreign security support constrain Maputo's effective control over gas-producing territory and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Consortium Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain substantial influence over project timing, revenues, and security arrangements.

highlights: Oil discoveries reshape strategic bargaining power
Green hydrogen ambitions attract major external capital

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Control
frictionVectors.details: Large offshore discoveries could strengthen national revenues, but licensing terms and operator dependence will determine how much value remains domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen infrastructure creates opportunities while exposing Namibia to infrastructure and offtake dependence.

highlights: Junta pushes resource nationalism and regional autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is challenging historic French-linked mining arrangements and seeking greater state participation, but technical and financial capacity remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Borderland Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence across the Sahel continues to threaten mining routes, energy infrastructure, and the government's practical authority beyond major cities.

highlights: Oil-sector reform faces persistent security leakage

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, militant activity, and vandalism reduce public revenues and limit effective state control over producing regions and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International oil firms remain important for deepwater investment and technology, while financing conditions constrain Abuja's bargaining leverage.

highlights: Eastern Congo tensions raise reputational and supply risks

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Allegations concerning mineral flows linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo expose Rwanda to diplomatic pressure and tighter traceability demands.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Aid Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control, but reliance on foreign investment, aid, and security partnerships creates leverage for outside actors.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Potential offshore hydrocarbons attract foreign energy interests, but limited discoveries and weak state capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power. Maritime surveillance and licensing transparency remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support from Portugal, China, and multilateral lenders provide needed capacity while limiting fiscal autonomy. Debt sustainability and project selection remain recurring concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Senegal greater fiscal leverage, but efforts to increase state participation and review legacy contracts risk friction with international operators and investors. Managing revenues transparently is central to sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and multilateral financing remains important for transport and energy projects. Senegal is seeking diversification, but repayment obligations and strategic port access create leverage for external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime-zone competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles' extensive maritime area is valuable for fisheries, tourism, seabed resources, and security partnerships. Limited enforcement capacity leaves the country dependent on foreign naval and technical support.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure and debt leverage
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf partners, and Western institutions compete for influence through infrastructure, connectivity, and security assistance. Victoria generally preserves room to maneuver, but its narrow fiscal base limits strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore and other mineral projects generate export earnings but leave Sierra Leone exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and uneven domestic value capture. Contract transparency and local processing remain contentious.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, energy, and mining logistics projects can improve connectivity while tying strategic infrastructure to external commercial interests. Debt, concession terms, and local employment are persistent pressure points.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil licensing
frictionVectors.details: Federal efforts to develop offshore hydrocarbons and attract international operators could expand state revenue, but opaque licensing, federal-regional disputes, and weak enforcement risk external capture. Maritime insecurity further complicates exploration.

frictionVectors.title: Security and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, Western partners, and other external actors provide military, port, and infrastructure support. These partnerships strengthen state capacity but can fragment strategic control over ports, coastal resources, and security policy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Chronic failures at Transnet constrain coal, iron-ore and container exports, weakening South Africa's control over strategic supply chains. Private-sector participation is advancing, but implementation remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Major-power competition
frictionVectors.details: Pretoria is balancing relations with China, the United States, Russia and Gulf investors while seeking value addition in critical minerals. This creates pressure over sanctions, technology access and ownership rules.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese pipelines and export infrastructure, leaving its primary revenue stream vulnerable to conflict, sabotage and bargaining by external transit authorities.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and foreign resource capture
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and opaque oil contracting limit sovereign control, while neighboring states, traders and security networks compete for access to crude and other commodities.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized gold economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance competing armed actors and connect Sudanese extraction zones to regional and Gulf trading networks. State institutions have little effective oversight across major mining areas.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and port contest
frictionVectors.details: Fighting around transport corridors, refineries and Port Sudan threatens national control of exports and humanitarian access. External military and commercial interests are deepening the fragmentation of critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LNG contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is using negotiations over its large offshore gas project to seek stronger domestic benefits, but delays and investor demands could limit value capture and fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam port and regional rail corridors are attracting Gulf, Chinese and other foreign capital. Tanzania must balance modernization needs with concerns over strategic dependence and local-content enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's port and trading corridors are vital to Togo's sovereignty and revenue base but remain heavily dependent on foreign shipping, logistics and finance networks. Regional instability could disrupt transit flows.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and insecurity in the Sahel threaten northern communities, transport routes and state access to resources. Foreign security assistance is increasingly important, creating sovereignty and accountability trade-offs.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia’s dependence on European budget support and migration cooperation gives the EU significant influence over domestic and foreign-policy choices. Disputes over migrant treatment and irregular departures periodically threaten the relationship.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported hydrocarbons and limited investment in domestic production constrain Tunisia’s policy autonomy. Phosphate-sector disruption further reduces export earnings and fiscal room.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP External-Control Concerns
frictionVectors.details: The TotalEnergies-led and Chinese-financed oil pipeline ties Uganda’s export infrastructure to foreign capital, contractors, and transit arrangements through Tanzania. Land acquisition, environmental concerns, and project delays continue to generate sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure borrowing and reliance on external security partnerships narrow Kampala’s fiscal and diplomatic flexibility. Oil development could improve leverage, but production revenues remain years away from fully offsetting these constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt are drawing intensified competition among Chinese, Western, Gulf, and regional investors. Zambia is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns, but foreign ownership and technology dependence limit immediate control.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and constrained rail and road corridors threaten mineral expansion and increase reliance on neighboring transit states. New external financing can relieve bottlenecks while also creating fresh repayment and strategic dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese investment remains prominent in lithium and other minerals, while Western and regional actors compete for access to Zimbabwe’s resource base. Export restrictions and beneficiation demands have increased state leverage, but limited domestic capital and processing capacity keep the country dependent.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent monetary instability, power shortages, and weak transport infrastructure force reliance on external finance and private operators. Sanctions, debt arrears, and uncertain property protections further reduce the government’s ability to capture stable resource rents.
